dedupe_keys.name: the watermachine at kristalbad enschede and hengelo multifunctional flood storage area

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes Kristalbad, a 40-hectare area between Enschede and Hengelo in the east of the Netherlands, redeveloped with the Watermachine concept, originally from Sweden, which uses natural processes to manage both floods and droughts. The area is divided into interconnected compartments that are filled in turn with water from the Elsebeek stream; together they store about 187,000 cubic metres during heavy rain to protect the two cities, purify water through wetland vegetation, release it to farmland in dry periods, link ecological corridors and provide recreation. Planning and design ran from 2005 to 2010, construction from 2010 to 2014, and monitoring continues; redevelopment cost about 6 million euros, excluding land purchase, with national, regional and local public funding. The page, published in 2017 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal with a link to the Water Board Vechtstromen. Caveats: evaluation against the objectives was still under way, and land costs are not included. It illustrates nature-based flood and drought hazard reduction and climate adaptation of urban edge water systems; related records are the Room for the River Regge, Serchio nature-based solutions and Isar-Plan case studies.
name: The Watermachine at Kristalbad (Enschede and Hengelo), multifunctional flood storage area
notes: Municipal involvement is inferred from the page's statement that local, regional and national policymakers were involved from the start.
organisations: Water Board Regge and Dinkel (now Vechtstromen)
outcomes: A 40 ha multifunctional area stores about 187,000 m3 of floodwater for Enschede and Hengelo, improves water quality and supplies water to farms in dry spells.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study based on Water Board Regge and Dinkel (now Vechtstromen) sources
